question: What is the difference between Creational, Structural, and Behavioral design patterns?
title: Creational vs Structural vs Behavioral Patterns
direct_answer: Creational patterns control object creation, Structural patterns define how objects compose, and Behavioral patterns define how objects communicate and distribute responsibility.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have a mental model for categorizing patterns — not just memorized names
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing pattern names without explaining the category distinction
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give 2 examples per category and say which problem each category addresses

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the Gang of Four categorized patterns into three groups based on what aspect of design they address. I would explain each:

'Creational patterns answer: how do I create objects? The issue is that direct instantiation (new SomeClass()) creates tight coupling to a specific class. Creational patterns decouple the creation from the usage.'

'Creational examples: Factory (let a method decide which concrete class to instantiate — you ask for a Shape, you get a Circle or Square without knowing which). Builder (construct complex objects step by step). Singleton (ensure only one instance exists). Abstract Factory (create families of related objects).'

'Structural patterns answer: how do objects and classes fit together to form larger structures?'

'Structural examples: Decorator (add behavior by wrapping). Adapter (translate one interface to another — legacy system integration). Facade (provide a simple interface to a complex subsystem). Proxy (provide a stand-in with access control, caching, or logging).'

'Behavioral patterns answer: how do objects communicate and who is responsible for what?'

'Behavioral examples: Strategy (interchangeable algorithms). Observer (one-to-many notification). Command (encapsulate a request as an object — undo and redo). Template Method (define algorithm skeleton, defer steps to subclasses).'

'Quick recall tip: Creational = who creates. Structural = how they fit. Behavioral = how they talk.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: Creational: control object creation — Factory, Builder, Singleton, Abstract Factory
Structural: how objects compose into structures — Decorator, Adapter, Facade, Proxy
Behavioral: how objects communicate — Strategy, Observer, Command, Template Method
Memory aid: Creational = who creates, Structural = how they fit, Behavioral = how they talk
Most commonly tested at fresher level: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Decorator
Patterns solve recurring problems — the category tells you which dimension of the problem

What is the Proxy pattern and how does it differ from Decorator?

question: How do you recognize which design pattern applies to a given problem?
title: How to Recognize Which Design Pattern to Apply
direct_answer: Identify the core problem: object creation (Creational), object composition (Structural), or object communication (Behavioral) — then match to the specific pattern signal within that group.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason about pattern selection rather than just memorize names
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Naming a pattern without explaining why it fits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a problem-to-pattern mapping: 'I see an if-else on types → Strategy. I see one-to-many notification → Observer. I see class explosion → Decorator.'

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So pattern recognition is a skill you build by seeing the problem signals. I would walk through the key signals:

'If-else on type to select behavior → Strategy. Multiple payment methods with different logic, multiple sort algorithms — any time you are switching on a type to do different things, Strategy replaces the switch.'

'One-to-many notification — event happens, multiple components need to react → Observer. Order placed, notify email + analytics + warehouse. The publisher should not know who is listening.'

'Complex object with many optional fields → Builder. Constructors with 6+ parameters, many are optional, want immutability.'

'Need to add behavior to an object without changing its class, behaviors are combinable → Decorator. Adding logging + caching + retry to a service.'

'Need exactly one instance, global point of access → Singleton. But use carefully — overused Singleton is a design smell.'

'Need to create objects without specifying the exact class → Factory. The creation logic belongs in one place and the caller just says give me a shape.'

'How to apply this in interviews: when the problem is described, I list the patterns that came to mind and explain which signals I saw. That process is more impressive than just saying the right name.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: If-else on type to select behavior → Strategy
One-to-many notification → Observer
Complex object with optional fields → Builder
Add behavior to objects without changing class, behaviors combine → Decorator
Need one instance, global access → Singleton (use sparingly)
Create objects without specifying class → Factory
In interviews: explain the signal you saw, not just the pattern name

question: What is the over-engineering anti-pattern and how do you avoid it with design patterns?
title: Avoiding Over-Engineering with Design Patterns
direct_answer: Over-engineering is applying patterns before there is a clear problem to solve — use YAGNI and start simple, adding patterns only when the specific problem they solve appears.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you have judgment about when patterns hurt rather than help
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating patterns as always positive — applying all patterns you know to a simple problem
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name YAGNI and give a concrete example of unnecessary pattern use

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So this is a mature engineering topic — knowing when NOT to use patterns is as important as knowing the patterns. I would explain it like this:

'Over-engineering is adding complexity before it is needed. Patterns are tools for solving specific problems. If the problem does not exist yet, applying the pattern adds complexity with no benefit.'

'Example: for a service that has one payment method and will not get another, adding a PaymentStrategy interface is over-engineering. You have created an interface, an implementation, and a context class — 3 entities instead of 1. If you never need a second payment method, this was wasted effort.'

'The YAGNI principle — You Aren t Gonna Need It — says: do not add abstraction for hypothetical future requirements. Add it when the concrete need arises.'

'In an LLD interview, I start simple and add patterns when the problem calls for it. If the interviewer says now add a second payment method, I introduce Strategy at that point — not preemptively. This shows I understand patterns as problem-solving tools, not things to apply by default.'

'Signs of over-engineering in design: interfaces with only one implementation ever; factory classes for creating objects with no variation; Observer with only one observer; abstract classes with no shared behavior. These are patterns applied without a problem to solve.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: YAGNI: do not add abstractions for hypothetical future requirements
Patterns are tools for specific problems — no problem, no pattern needed
Over-engineering signals: interface with one impl, factory with no variation, Observer with one observer
Start simple; introduce patterns when the specific problem they solve appears
In LLD interviews: add patterns reactively when the interviewer introduces the problem
Over-used patterns add complexity, reduce readability, increase onboarding time

followup_questions: What is premature abstraction and why is it harmful?

question: When does simple code beat using a design pattern?
title: When Simple Code Beats Design Patterns
direct_answer: Simple code wins when the problem has only one variation, the codebase is small, or the pattern abstraction cost exceeds the flexibility gained.

interviewer_intent.testing: Engineering pragmatism — experienced developers know patterns have costs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking patterns are always better than simple code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a specific trade-off: 'For this case, a 3-line if-else is clearer than introducing Strategy pattern with 3 new files'

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So engineering judgment includes knowing when to skip the pattern. I would frame it this way:

'Every pattern has a cost: more files, more abstraction layers, higher cognitive load for new team members. The pattern pays off when the benefit (flexibility, extensibility, decoupling) outweighs the cost.'

'Simple if-else beats Strategy when: there are 2 cases and there is little chance of a third. A 3-line if-else is readable. Adding Strategy means: 1 interface, 2 implementation classes, a context class, possibly a factory. That is 4+ files for 2 cases that will not change.'

'Simple constructor beats Builder when: the object has 3 required fields and no optional ones. Point(x, y, z) is clear. Builder adds an inner class and 4+ methods for no readability gain.'

'Simple inheritance beats Decorator when: you need exactly one added behavior, not N combinable behaviors. LoggingService extends RealService is clearer than a decorator chain of one.'

'The questions I ask: Will this actually need to vary? How often will it change? Does the pattern make the code more or less readable for a new team member? If the pattern makes the code harder to read without clear extensibility benefit — skip it.'

'In an interview, showing this judgment is a positive signal. Saying I would use a simple approach here because X is one variation and we have no indication it will change shows pragmatic engineering thinking.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: Every pattern has a cost: files, abstraction, cognitive load
2 cases that will not grow → if-else beats Strategy
3 required fields, no optionals → constructor beats Builder
One added behavior, no combinations → inheritance beats Decorator
Ask: will this vary? How often? Does abstraction improve or reduce readability?
Showing restraint about patterns is a sign of engineering maturity

question: How do you approach 'design pattern' questions in a Java interview?
title: Interview Strategy for Design Pattern Questions
direct_answer: Identify the problem signal → name the pattern category → explain the specific pattern → connect to a real Java or Spring example → note when it would be overkill.

interviewer_intent.testing: Meta-awareness and communication — can you structure a complete pattern answer?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving only a textbook definition without connecting to real code or trade-offs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Add: 'I would use this when X, but not when Y' — showing judgment is the highest signal

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So when a design patterns question comes up in an interview, here is the structure I use:

'Step 1: Name the problem it solves. Do not start with the definition — start with the problem. For Strategy: The problem is that if-else chains for selecting behavior violate OCP and become hard to extend. For Observer: The problem is tight coupling when multiple components need to react to the same event.'

'Step 2: Explain the pattern structure in one sentence. Strategy defines a family of algorithms behind an interface and makes them interchangeable.'

'Step 3: Show a real Java or Spring example. For Strategy: Comparator in Java, PasswordEncoder in Spring Security. For Observer: @EventListener in Spring, ActionListener in Swing.'

'Step 4: Give a concrete domain example. For Strategy: payment methods in a checkout flow. For Observer: order placed event notifying email, analytics, and warehouse services.'

'Step 5: Note when you would NOT use it. For Strategy: if there is only one payment method and that will not change. For Observer: if there is only one listener and it will not be dynamic.'

'This 5-step answer takes about 2-3 minutes. The last step — when not to use it — is what separates a senior-thinking answer from a textbook recitation.'

sections.title: Key Points
content: Start with the problem the pattern solves — not the definition
One-sentence structural description: 'X pattern does Y by Z'
Real Java or Spring example: Comparator, @EventListener, PasswordEncoder
Domain example: payment, notification, fee calculation
Always close with when NOT to use it — shows engineering judgment
5-step answer: problem → structure → Java example → domain example → trade-off
